description: We are a team of six passionate programmers who want to bring forth a revolution in agriculture with our skills and NASA's support.
summary:
A voice-first farming companion for rainfed smallholder farmers in Pothohar, Pakistan.
Kisan Saathi helps farmers make timely, practical decisions throughout the wheat-growing season. The project brings together NASA Earth-observation datasets, regional agronomy guidance, Urdu-first assistance, and simple tools for tracking field health and food-loss prevention.
Seasonal crop roadmap — guided stages for sowing, tillering, pest scouting, grain filling, and harvest, with clear progress states and actionable advisories.
Earth-observation context — uses datasets and products including NASA SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG precipitation, Harmonized Landsat–Sentinel (HLS), NASA POWER, ECOSTRESS, and NASADEM.
Barkat tracker — illustrates estimated food loss prevented and explains the assumptions behind the estimate.
Season history — connects current conditions with previous-season notes and outcomes.
Summer crop planning — compares summer fallow, mungbean, and sorghum fodder against priorities such as water, income, soil health, and cattle feed.
Field health — visualizes vegetation-health trends, including NDVI comparisons.
Ask Kisan Saathi — an Urdu AI assistance experience for farmer questions.
Demo timeline — lets users move through the crop season and see how roadmap guidance changes.
The primary Android application is built with Kotlin and Jetpack Compose. Also contains a Flutter client; its current configuration uses mock repository and voice-service implementations by default.
details:
Kisan Saathi: Project Report

15 Nov 2026 · @JabirShrif

Summary

Kisan Saathi is an Android app that tells rainfed wheat farmers in Pakistan's Pothohar region what to do, by when and why, in Urdu that can be read aloud. The team built the app interface, an advisory engine that runs on 20 years of real weather data, a backend API and one small soil moisture model.

Three results stand out:

  • Sowing date drives heat risk. Replaying 21 seasons of Chakwal weather, a crop sown on 9 November meets five or more hot days at grain fill in 14% of years. Sown on 29 November, it does so in 38% of years.
  • One planned data source could not be used as intended. NASA POWER rainfall for Chakwal roughly doubles from 2020 while two independent sources do not, so rainfall and temperature were taken from other sources.
  • Real rainfed yields are far below the app's first assumption. Chakwal's rainfed wheat averaged 17.9 maund per acre over five reported seasons, against an assumed 32.

The engine is tested and matches between server and phone. Connecting it to every app screen, adding satellite crop greenness, and verifying the agronomy thresholds with local experts are still to do.

Problem

Rainfed (barani) wheat farmers in Pothohar have no canal or tube well, so a few decisions made on the wrong day can cost much of the harvest.

  • Sowing. Seed sown into dry soil emerges patchily. Seed sown late pushes grain filling into the heat of March.
  • Fertiliser. Urea applied to dry ground is wasted, and urea applied before heavy rain washes away.
  • Protection. Farmers often spray at the first sign of a pest, whether or not the infestation justifies it. A storm on a ripe crop can spoil grain days before storage.

Satellites and weather models already measure rainfall, temperature and soil conditions over these fields. That information sits in technical archives, in English, and does not reach the farmer as a decision on the day it matters. Limited literacy makes even written advisories hard to use.

Solution

Kisan Saathi gives the farmer one advisory card at a time: the action, the deadline and the evidence behind it. Every card is available in Urdu and English and can be read aloud.

Barkat is calculated as expected yield × field area × the loss fraction the action avoids. The loss fractions are placeholders until trial results are available, and the app labels them as such.

System design

[embed: node/863344a0-7f7a]

Because the server and the phone read the same bundle and apply the same rules, a phone with no signal gives the same advice as the server. The bundle is rebuilt by rerunning the pipeline whenever new data is downloaded.

Data

The engine runs on daily records from 1 January 2005 to 12 November 2026 for three grid cells around Chakwal, plus a 7-day forecast. All of it was downloaded on 15 November 2026.

MODIS crop greenness and SMAP soil moisture were requested from NASA AppEEARS but had not arrived when this report was written.

NASA POWER is not consistent across 2020 for Chakwal

Checking the three weather sources against each other showed a break in NASA POWER at 2020.

POWER rainfall roughly doubles from 2020 while both other sources do not, so the change is in POWER and not in the weather. The cause was not investigated. Rainfall was therefore taken from IMERG, temperature from ERA5, and only POWER's pre-2020 wetness was used for training.

Models and results

One model was trained and kept, one was tried and dropped, and one could not be trained for lack of data.

Soil moisture model

The model estimates surface wetness from the last 30 days of rainfall and evaporation, then multiplies by soil porosity (0.468 at Dhudial) to give volumetric moisture. It is a small gradient-boosted tree model, about 77 KB as text, trained on 2005 to 2015 and tested on 2016 to 2019.

Measure on the test years

Model

Mean absolute error, wetness on a 0 to 1 scale

The model beats a seasonal average but is modest. Its error is about 0.03 m³/m³ of moisture, against a sowing window 0.15 wide. With forecast rain as input it also gives a 3-day and 7-day outlook.

Heat risk by sowing date

[embed: node/829b8a0c-99f3]

For each sowing date, 21 seasons of weather were replayed and the hot days between flowering and maturity were counted. This is a climatology table, not a trained model, and it is quoted inside the sowing advisory.

A classifier that tried to predict a hot grain-fill from mid-February conditions scored 38% in leave-one-out testing, below the 50% of a coin flip. It was dropped.

District wheat yield

Chakwal's rainfed wheat averaged 17.9 maund per acre across five reported seasons. The engine uses that figure for Barkat in place of the app's earlier assumption of 32, which is close to the irrigated yield.

Advisory rules

Seven groups of rules turn the day's conditions into cards. Every threshold is a draft taken from the project's configuration and has not been verified by an agronomist.

Rule

Fires when

Advice

Sowing

Not yet sown, between 20 Oct and 15 Dec

Sow within 3 days if soil moisture is 20 to 35%; wait if drier, wetter, or if 20 mm or more of rain is due in 2 days. Quotes the heat risk for sowing now against 10 days later.

Urea top-dress

Crop is tillering (450 to 750 growing degree days)

Apply if the soil is moist or a light shower has just fallen; hold if 10 mm or more of rain is due in 2 days; wait if dry.

Frost

December to February, forecast minimum below 2 °C in 3 nights

Check low-lying parts of the field.

Aphid scouting

Jointing to flowering, weekly mean 15 to 28 °C, humidity 60% or more

Check 20 plants in 4 spots before any spray.

Yellow rust scouting

Tillering to flowering, weekly mean 10 to 22 °C, humidity 75% or more

Inspect lower leaves on a damp morning.

Terminal heat

Heading or flowering, forecast maximum 32 °C or more in 5 days

Warn, and note the season for next year's sowing date.

Harvest

Crop has reached maturity (2,000 growing degree days)

Harvest if 3 dry days are ahead; otherwise protect the crop from the coming rain.

The engine never names a pesticide or a dose. Pest rules only ask the farmer to scout and to consult the extension officer. For past dates, the "forecast" in each rule is the weather that actually followed, which lets any day since October 2019 be replayed.

Testing

The engine and backend were tested; the final connection into the Android app was not.

The tests include physical checks, for example that estimated soil moisture rises after rain, that heat risk rises with later sowing, and that no advisory text contains a pesticide prescription.

SDG alignment

The project is designed to support five Sustainable Development Goals, with SDG 2 as the primary one. These are design aims; no impact has been measured yet.

Goal

How the project supports it

SDG 2: Zero Hunger

Better-timed sowing, fertiliser and harvest aim to raise yields and cut avoidable losses for smallholders

SDG 6: Clean Water and Sanitation

Soil moisture estimates show how much water the field already holds

SDG 12: Responsible Consumption and Production

Advice steers farmers away from fertiliser and pesticide they do not need

SDG 13: Climate Action

Weather-aware advice and the heat-risk table help farmers adapt to erratic rain and heat

SDG 15: Life on Land

Crop and soil monitoring, and a summer crop in place of bare fallow, support sustainable land use

There is an indirect link to SDG 1, No Poverty, through farm income.

Limitations and next steps

The engine works on real data, but several parts of the product still rest on estimates, drafts or demo values.

Limitations

  • Soil moisture is a model estimate from rainfall and evaporation. It has not been checked against SMAP or a field probe, and its error is about a fifth of the width of the sowing window.
  • Every agronomy threshold is a draft, and the Barkat loss fractions are placeholders.
  • The draft maturity threshold looks too low: a crop sown on 10 November reaches it in late March, about three weeks before Chakwal's usual harvest. This shortens the grain-fill window used in the heat-risk table.
  • Weather comes from grid cells of roughly 10 to 50 km, not from the individual field.
  • The Field Health, Summer Planner, History and Rewards screens still show demo values.
  • Ask and photo scan depend on Google Gemini and need a connection.
  • The backend has no login, database or user storage.

Next steps

  • Connect the engine to the app's advisory screen and build the APK.
  • Add MODIS crop greenness for the Field Health screen once the AppEEARS files arrive.
  • Retrain the soil moisture model against SMAP.
  • Download weather for Attock, Rawalpindi and Jhelum, add the missing 2022-23 yields, and attempt a yield model.
  • Have BARI Chakwal or Punjab extension staff review the thresholds, starting with maturity.
  • Replace the summer planner placeholders with market prices and a crop-model run.
  • Pilot with a small group of farmers.

Team and sources

Team BlackWater: Jabir Sharif, Sohayel Mahmud, Tauhidur Rahman Shishir, Md Tasnimul Hasan Zihad, Ishtiaq Mahmud and Ekramul Islam.

Code repository: github.com/starbucksat4thave/Kisan-Saathi-BlackWater-

Data sources

  • NASA GPM IMERG daily precipitation, Final Run (GPM_3IMERGDF v07), retrieved through NASA Giovanni
  • NASA POWER agroclimatology daily data
  • Open-Meteo historical weather (ERA5) and forecast
  • SoilGrids, ISRIC
  • Punjab Crop Reporting Service: Rabi Final Estimates 2020-21, Final Rabi Estimates 2021-22, and Final Rabi Estimates 2024-25

All figures in this report were computed from files downloaded on 15 November 2026. The technology stack is Kotlin with Jetpack Compose and Firebase for the app, and Python with FastAPI and scikit-learn for the engine and backend.
